article.title: “U.S. Policy Will Change Before Cubans Tire of Defending Our Sovereignty”: Cuban Foreign Minister
article.author: MLToday
article.content: CUBADEBATE November 5, 2026 N.Y. Times Journalist Jack Nicas: What is the status of the talks between your government and the United States? When was the last time you spoke, and who is involved? Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla: Yes, the talks continue, but without significant results or much progress. Given the coercive nature of the policy that the United States government is currently applying very intensely against Cuba, and given that it is very difficult for talks to progress when they are constantly accompanied by threats and the application of unilateral coercive measures—military threats, threats of a military nature, or even fuel blockades, which are equivalent to a naval blockade, an act of war—and a series of actions that constitute an act of collective punishment under International Law. Therefore, our willingness to continue these talks remains, with the aim of finding solutions to bilateral issues based on international law, sovereign equality, on an equal footing, without interference in internal affairs, and on the basis of mutual respect and reciprocal benefit. I need not go into too much detail, but I confirm that talks have taken place and that the Cuban side remains willing to continue. Journalist : I understand you don’t want to go into some specific details, but what are the channels like, to understand, are they face-to-face conversations or by phone, what are they like? Minister: Yes, as I was saying, I preferred not to go into details. These are political-level talks in which the Cuban side has maintained a constant willingness to move forward in resolving bilateral problems, some of them long-standing and others stemming from the hardening of the US government’s policy against Cuba, which is causing extraordinary humanitarian damage. Journalist: Except that your Chargé d’Affaires in Washington said there are channels such as meetings, calls, and WhatsApp messages. Can you confirm that? Minister: If the Chargé d’Affaires said so, I don’t need to confirm it. Journalist: Have you spoken this month, in October? Minister: I told him I preferred not to go into details, but talks have been ongoing for some time without major results and I hope they will continue. Journalist: The White House has said there needs to be political change. Your administration has made it clear that this isn’t going to happen and that it’s not appropriate to discuss such a matter. Where is there room for negotiation? What, if anything, is your administration willing to concede? Minister: Imagine if the Cuban government were to say that for talks with the United States to take place, there must be political change in the United States. Furthermore, the United States government does not apply a single standard on this issue because it maintains excellent relations with countries that have governments, political systems, and electoral systems—or even lack them altogether—completely different from U.S. standards. Third, no political difference could justify a siege like the one being waged against Cuba today. No political difference could be a sufficient pretext for imposing a fuel blockade against a small, peace-loving nation; and no political reason could justify acts of collective punishment that cause harm, pain, suffering, and anguish to all Cuban families. I can tell you that we, too, have concerns regarding the American political system. We don’t like their model of democracy, but we persist in the idea of a plurality of political models, a plurality of democratic models, based on the plurality of cultures that exist on the planet. We do not agree with the idea of a single way of thinking, a single model, a single culture, and even less so that this culture should be modeled on the dysfunctional American democracy. But this is not a matter for our bilateral discussions. It should not be an obstacle to making progress in resolving long-standing or more recent bilateral issues. For example, Cuba has always been willing to address issues that are of interest and benefit to the national interest of the United States and especially to the American people. For example, Cuba has provided and will continue to provide its full cooperation in law enforcement and compliance, in relation to national or joint efforts against terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, and international organized crime, and in support of a satisfactory migration relationship between the two countries. There are numerous areas, well, there are still 22 bilateral cooperation agreements in force in areas that are of the greatest interest to both nations and should be of the greatest interest to both governments, and we are fully prepared to continue efforts in that regard. For example, in the area of counterterrorism, Cuba has made significant efforts in relation to the latest act of terrorism against Cuba, which was the attempted infiltration of Cuban territory by a heavily armed terrorist cell equipped with weapons of war, explosives, and communications equipment. We have offered the United States government a joint investigation into this matter. And there are long-standing issues, such as the matter of mutual compensation, stemming from the nationalizations of U.S. properties in Cuba, carried out under both Cuban and U.S. law. These nationalizations were recognized by the U.S. Supreme Court in the Sabatino case, for example, as lawful, but the owners were unable to receive compensation precisely because of the obstacles and historical antagonism of the U.S. government. And in Cuba, there are also rulings by Cuban courts demanding compensation from the U.S. government for economic and human damages suffered by Cuba during these 60 years of bilateral conflict. Journalist: I think your position is very reasonable, but the situation is that the White House isn’t necessarily very reasonable in this situation, so it’s clear they’re asking for political changes, things you don’t want to discuss. It seems like the things on the table for you are about, well, aid on terrorism, things like that, also maybe reparations, and maybe economic reforms. Are they asking for specific things regarding political or economic changes right now, or do they seem satisfied with these concessions on terrorism, things like that? Minister: Well, it’s difficult to say; that would be a good question for the U.S. side. But I can tell you that Cuba is currently engaged in very important changes to its economic model. These changes are not the result of talks or requests from the U.S. government, but rather stem from our own realities and our desire to ensure the well-being and prosperity of our people. Of course, the international economic environment has become very challenging due to global changes; and secondly, because the Cuban economy must necessarily adapt to this economic war being waged by the U.S. government. But I have always thought that in the area of economic relations, investment, travel – I don’t say tourism because it is prohibited by US law – in relations between US citizens and Cuba, in the area of health, in the area of the biomedical or pharmaceutical industry and in others, there are great possibilities to advance for the benefit of both peoples. A few months ago, Cuba launched a program of changes to its economic model, which are not aimed at fulfilling any requests in this regard, but which open up additional opportunities for US companies to do business with Cuban counterparts. These changes will take into account the interests of U.S. companies based on their merit and competitiveness. In other words, there will be neither privileges nor discrimination for U.S. companies that wish to take advantage of this opportunity. In 2018, over 600,000 Americans and over 400,000 Cubans residing in the United States traveled to Cuba. A thriving private industry developed around these trips, but it later suffered the consequences of the cessation and prohibition of these operations. More recently, the United States government, as it does almost every other Thursday, has taken decisions that further restrict Americans’ right to travel freely, particularly their right to travel to our country, by eliminating certain licenses that, until now, allowed such travel, albeit in a very limited way. In recent years, Cuba has experienced significant growth in its private sector, with a rise in small and medium-sized enterprises that are entirely privately owned. Extensive opportunities have opened up for Cubans living abroad, including in the United States, to participate in these businesses, and ample opportunities are being offered to foreign investors. The United States should not be allowed to control sectors of the Cuban economy to the detriment of its international competitors in this area, but the presence of its companies, which we recognize as competitive, would be welcome in the Cuban economy. For example, in the health and biomedical-pharmaceutical sectors, Cuba also has comparative advantages. It has some therapeutic vaccines, in some cases unique or among the most successful, for treating head, neck, and lung cancer. It has a treatment unique in the world for diabetes, particularly for preventing amputations resulting from diabetic foot ulcers. It has very innovative medications for treating degenerative neurological diseases, including Alzheimer’s, and has a wide range of treatments and experience in the production of new technologies, possessing technologies that are currently unique. Why not encourage this cooperation? Why deprive Americans of these options that we know are of interest to American companies, or even to patient associations, medical associations, or groups of people? Secondly, what political pretext could justify preventing a Cuban child with cancer from accessing the best treatments, or even the specific, appropriate treatment, which in some cases is exclusively American and protected by American patents? How can we prevent a newborn from accessing less invasive treatments for genetic heart conditions using American medical devices, technologies, or equipment that are virtually exclusive to the world? There is no way to justify that, in a politically motivated manner, which is the core of this administration’s US policy against Cuba, which is to create despair, anguish, suffering, and pain in the population with the aim of destabilizing the country and provoking a regime change. I don’t know if you are familiar with a 1960 memorandum from an Under Secretary of State in the Eisenhower administration, Lester Mallory. I suggest you look it up. It was a classified document for 30 years, but it remains the main orientation of US policy against Cuba, which recognizes the majority support of the Cuban people for the constitutional order that has been established in several free and universal referendums, because in Cuba the Constitution and fundamental laws are submitted to popular referendum and have been freely and sovereignly chosen by our people. That memorandum recognizes that the way to alienate the majority consensus of the Cuban people is precisely by causing suffering, and that this is what allows us to affirm in a technical-legal, not rhetorical, way that the economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed against Cuba is classified as an act of genocide according to the Geneva Convention and is classified as an act of collective punishment according to International Law, International Human Rights Law or even International Humanitarian Law, which is used only in times of military conflict. The fuel blockade is tantamount to a hostile act, an act of war under International Humanitarian Law, causing devastating humanitarian damage. For example, Cuba’s health indicators are currently comparable to those of developed countries, yet they reflect these impacts. Infant mortality—that is, the mortality rate of children under five years of age born alive, which is considered one of the most representative indicators of human development and the health and well-being of a population—is currently 9.9 per 1,000 live births. This is comparable to developed countries, but this rate has doubled in recent years due to these extreme blockade measures, because our regular rate was around 4 per 1,000 live births. The life expectancy of children with cancer in Cuba was among the highest in the world, at 85%, but it has fallen to 65%. Health indicators show a decline in the levels of timely and early immunization of children against communicable diseases, in the monitoring of pregnant women (with studies that are very thorough in Cuba), and in the country’s overall mortality data, all of which are effects of this cruel and inhumane policy. There could be highly beneficial alliances between U.S. institutions and Cuban institutions, which are among the most competitive in the world in the biomedical and pharmaceutical fields, to cooperate on treatments for both communicable and non-communicable diseases. Cuba was able to produce five COVID-19 vaccines in record time and with minimal resources, guaranteeing immunity for our population and achieving some of the best results in the world in confronting that pandemic. Journalist: The relationship between your country and the United States is very unequal, very, very unequal. The United States is much more powerful, much richer, much larger, and they are currently very aggressive toward you. They want political change, and you haven’t seen almost any allies coming to your aid. So it’s a very, very serious situation, and your people are suffering. So, what is your strategy for getting out of this situation? Minister: Well, imagine what the United States government would do if, 90 miles from the United States, there were a global superpower far larger than the United States, in the same proportion as the US economy, its Gross Domestic Product, its armed forces, its weapons capabilities, including the existence of nuclear weapons, its territory, and its technological development. It would be a country that obviously doesn’t exist today, precisely because I agree with you on the enormous disproportion between the power of a small nation, a small island state with a developing economy subject to these circumstances, and this great nuclear superpower. What would the policies of a government like this be under those circumstances? How would American democracy function under those circumstances? How would the US economy function if this enormous, imaginary superpower, controlling finance, technology, and the global economy, pursued a regime change policy against the United States? Secondly, we should also consider the situation of other countries in our region or any other region, or even developed countries, that were subjected to a siege like this for 60 years, or that for the last five or six years had been subjected to an extreme blockade like this, or that for almost a year had been prevented from receiving fuel supplies. How many countries would have withstood it? How many governments would have remained in place? Which countries could have avoided a humanitarian catastrophe? People dying en masse in the streets, widespread famine. Yet Cuba has had the capacity to prevent that, to resist that, and to do so without giving up. I, too, have heard politicians… Journalist: Excuse me, but with all due respect, I understand perfectly, and I think it’s very reasonable, and the question isn’t about the ethics of Americans. We’ve already written about what Americans are doing, creating suffering in Cuba, but the question is what their strategy is for getting out of this situation. Minister: Yes, and I am responding to you. I am responding in the sense of trying to help New York Times readers understand that very few countries on the planet would have been able to have this conversation today, almost a year after the policies that have been applied against Cuba were implemented, especially since January 3 of this year, and yet there has not been a humanitarian catastrophe in Cuba; we have been able to prevent it. The Cuban economy has not collapsed. The state remains effective because the effectiveness of a state must be measured considering these oppressive circumstances. And I was saying that I’ve noticed some US politicians, including the Secretary of State, for example, have been lowering expectations regarding immediate regime change in Cuba. First they said it would be in a few weeks, then they said it would be immediately after what happened in early January in South America, then they said as soon as there was a pause in the war against Iran, then they said it would be before summer, during the summer. Someone said in 30 days we will control the Cuban economy. The president said we will take Cuba, we will control Cuba, friendly or unfriendly, immediately. And yet, the Secretary of State now explains that patience and time are needed, that this is a supposed problem that has existed for many decades and cannot be solved quickly, and he has proclaimed, therefore, that the objective of this US administration is not immediate regime change, but rather that Cuba be on an irreversible path of approximation to US interests. So, given this situation, one has to ask oneself, well, what is the reason—and it’s a question I’m frequently asked—why Cuba has been able to withstand this unprecedented pressure, because there has never been a sanctions regime anywhere in the world, in history, like the one that has been historically applied against Cuba, nor has there ever been, nor is there now, another comprehensive system of blockade and unilateral coercive measures against any country like the one being applied against Cuba today. For example, there is currently no country being prevented from receiving fuel supplies, and not only fuel supplies, but also because action has been taken against shipping companies—that is, maritime transport companies—forcing them to renege on signed and paid contracts. Most of these shipments contain perishable and essential goods such as food, medicine, and medical devices, and the majority of these shipments were contracted by the private sector, by small and medium-sized private companies in Cuba. These goods are currently located in various ports around the world because, faced with threats and sanctions, the shipping companies refuse to honor their contracts and deliver the goods to Cuban ports. This has jeopardized, for example, the hemodialysis treatments in Cuba for more than 3,000 patients. Hemodialysis treatments are a matter of life or death and cannot be postponed, yet we have been able to resolve this issue. We have an economic program, as I mentioned before, which is part of our strategy not only for survival but also for the recovery of our economic growth. Its main objective is the well-being of the population, guaranteeing social justice and social coverage, ensuring that no family or individual is left destitute. However, it also significantly changes the economic model, which will remain socialist but opens up many new opportunities for private capital, foreign investors, and companies from different countries. We would like to invite American companies to participate in these opportunities. Secondly, Cuba is receiving extraordinary international solidarity that encourages us, and US policy against Cuba is suffering enormous discredit and international isolation. If our strategy weren’t working, why then, last January, after exhausting five or six years of extreme blockade measures, had a total energy blockade been declared? If our strategy and our state were ineffective, why had secondary sanctions been added in May against all countries with ties to Cuba? Why, every other Thursday, have new sanctions been applied—some unimaginable, some even designed to impede Cuba’s international cooperation with other countries, such as Cuba’s international medical cooperation with African and Caribbean nations, from which Cuba receives no income? Because Cuba is an exporter of medical services, but it also has cooperation programs from which it receives no benefit. In other words, why do all this if the Cuban strategy and the Cuban state are considered ineffective? The day after tomorrow, that is, tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, the United Nations General Assembly will consider the issue of the blockade against Cuba and I am sure that it will approve with a large majority vote a resolution demanding that the United States unconditionally end the blockade against Cuba. If our strategy and our situation were not effective, why would the United States have had to dedicate itself in recent months, since June and in recent weeks in particular, across the globe, to threatening governments, threatening foreign ministries, deploying its ambassadors everywhere, the Secretary of State sending documents? I have some of those documents in my possession; some I have already shown, others I will show now in the General Assembly. They are terribly threatening documents, not only against governments but even against their readers, their recipients, because they threaten them directly. They require very careful reading and very thorough consideration, under penalty of applying sanctions to the governments and to you, the recipient and your family. Journalist: So, Minister, it seems to me that the strategy then… Minister: If the strategy didn’t work, we wouldn’t be talking here today. Journalist : I understand , but what’s the strategy? Is it survival? Is it to last? Is it to wait until the United States gets tired of it . Minister: The United States’ policy toward Cuba is going to change. It will have to change. It’s inevitable that it will change. Journalist: Why? Minister: First, because American citizens oppose it. All the polls from 2026 and all the online conversation studies in the United States, particularly in English, reflect around 70% opposition to the energy blockade and collective punishment. I don’t know about the New York Times, but I frequently encounter the terms “fuel blockade” and “collective punishment” in the mainstream American press, which is a new phenomenon. This is not only reflected in Cuban statements, but also in the language of American journalists and other individuals. Secondly, because the majority of Cubans residing in the United States, although many of them do not vote, also oppose this policy of collective punishment or even military threat against my country, just like American citizens. Third, because it’s a very old policy that hasn’t yielded the slightest result. In other words, for 60 years this policy hasn’t moved the United States, or successive administrations, one iota toward the goals each of them has proclaimed. It’s a policy that has failed for 60 years. It is a policy that has been taken to extremes to practically warlike levels; it is an economic war that has lasted for almost a year, which has not advanced the United States one millimeter towards the regime change goals it proclaimed. Journalist: But politics has lasted quite a while too . Minister: A lot. Journalist: So the question is, it seems your strategy is to survive, to last, and you’re achieving that. But the question then is, how much longer can you survive? Minister: Fourth, the policy will have to change because it runs counter to the national interest of the United States. What could the national interest of the United States possibly be regarding Cuba? To destabilize the Caribbean Basin? To destabilize the area where there are enormous oil investments by the United States and other regional partners in the Caribbean Basin? To destabilize the important maritime trade routes that supply the ports of the eastern United States? To destabilize the Caribbean and Central America? To generate an uncontrolled wave of migration to the United States? If the Cuban economy were to collapse, what would happen the next day? What would happen in relation to the United States? But I am answering your question, although you may think I am going on for too long, and perhaps you are in a hurry. But as I was saying, it contradicts the national interest of the United States. Furthermore, it only discredits and isolates the United States in terms of foreign policy. It undermines the United States’ national interest in the Americas and the Caribbean region. So, it must be acknowledged that, in these 60 years, up to today, October 26, the United States’ policy against Cuba has not worked, while Cuba’s policy of resistance and adaptation to that aggression has worked and has been successful. For how long? For as long as it takes. The United States’ policy will change sooner than we Cubans will tire of defending our independence, our sovereignty, our territorial integrity. This is an issue that dates back more than 100 years. In other words, this conflict did not begin with the Cuban Revolution. The United States’ desire to seize and dominate Cuba dates back to the 19th century. Journalist: Very well. I’m in no hurry, it’s just that he’s going to tell me… Minister: It’s the friend who’s in a hurry… I understand. Journalist: And it’s very important to get some specific and clear answers to get a story about that. Because five months ago your government said that Cuba’s oil had run out, but now in October you’re operating. Where is the oil coming from, and how much more? Minister: Well, almost half of the oil that the Cuban economy needs is produced in Cuba. We produce a crude oil that is very heavy and has a high sulfur content, which we couldn’t refine. Part of our strategy has been to develop our own refining technology. This is a fact. Another fact is that we have opened up possibilities for the private sector to import fuel, which are small because the United States government prevents the private sector from importing larger quantities of fuel, applying restriction after restriction and forcing them to do so only in very small, very limited quantities and at exorbitant prices. Journalist: How do you feel about receiving oil from the United States? Does it create a dependency? Minister: Perfectly. Well, it’s an idea that hasn’t been considered because there seems to be no danger of the Cuban economy becoming dependent on US fuel because US regulations prevent that possibility; they fiercely prevent it to this day. But what I want to tell you is that for us, having a presence on equal footing with European and other global companies in the Cuban economy would be desirable. Regarding energy, one factor that has allowed us to survive, and not only survive but also increase our capacity, is that despite the US embargo, we have achieved significant development in renewable energy, particularly photovoltaics, in record time. Today, during daylight hours, more than half of Cuba’s electricity generation comes from photovoltaic sources. So, that’s another factor in our adaptation. Journalist: Very well. Two more questions. The other thing is, are you counting on or expecting the US midterm elections to change your situation? Minister: That would be difficult to answer. First, the question is somewhat hypothetical because we don’t know the outcome of the election until the taxpayers, the American voters, cast their ballots in the first days of November. Second, because we would have to see how American democracy will function under whatever circumstances arise, whatever the possible results. But today it is a reality that the majority of American voters and the majority of American taxpayers oppose this policy. Hopefully, in any case, both the government and Congress will take into account the will of the American people. We will have to wait and see. Journalist : Isn’t this vote part of your hope or strategy that the situation will change? Minister: No, a matter that is entirely internal to the United States cannot be a variable in our strategy. Journalist: And finally, of course, you’ve seen this message from Rubio in which they’re looking for informants for the CIA. What do you think of a strategy that seeks informants in that way? And also this morning, the United States Ambassador to Cuba met with the Armed Forces, and they said there’s a lot to discuss regarding Cuba. What’s your opinion, what’s your reaction? Minister: Well, we would have to ask our American counterparts. It is known that, at the time, in addition to diplomatic talks with the State Department, there was contact between the U.S. and Cuban armed forces and between the Central Intelligence Agency and its Cuban counterparts. The truth is, I have no idea what the Secretary of State is trying to achieve with these publications, which frankly don’t seem serious at all; they seem a bit childish. And the truth is, I can’t understand why the Secretary of State is referring to public instructions from an intelligence agency asking Cubans to recruit them en masse and giving them directions that seem more like something out of a James Bond movie than reality. Journalist: To say those things publicly, do you think they’re trying to psychologically manipulate you or mess with you guys in some way? Minister: There is an unconventional war being waged against Cuba that has been part of these past 60 years. A war that today they call cognitive or fourth- or fifth-generation warfare, which they intend to wage not in a physical theater of operations, but now not only in cyberspace but also in people’s minds, in their very being. It won’t work because the Cuban people have, first of all, a high level of education. Secondly, because they have a very high level of information, and thirdly, because they have a high level of political awareness. They recognize who is responsible for the harm they are suffering, the consequences they are enduring, and the real causes of their suffering, anguish, and deprivation. They enjoy broad, intergenerational consensus at the social level. They feel that they are participating in the search for solutions, in the search for ways out, despite the Secretary of State’s repeated assertions that every time Cuba finds a way out, every time there is a valve, the US government will shut it down, will cut it off. But we Cubans feel like we’re participating in this process because Cuban culture is native, it’s powerful, because the idea of Cuban independence and sovereignty is practically ingrained, an essential part of our culture. The determination to defend our territorial integrity, our homeland, to the very end, at the grassroots level, is a cultural matter, shared by the vast majority of our population. But it is true that there is a very intense cognitive war against our country that is as illegal and inhumane as the fuel blockade or collective punishment or preventing shipping companies from bringing their merchandise to our country. Journalist: Very well, thank you very much. Do you have a little more time? One more question, or what? Minister: One more. Journalist : Well, about privatization. Minister: Excuse me? Journalist: On privatization. Minister: Privatization. Journalist: Thank you. “Privatization, privatization.” I believe his government calls the reforms “flexibilization,” not privatization. But it seems Cuba is selling shares in state-owned companies to Cubans and foreigners, and several other things are being privatized—gas stations and pharmacies are now privately owned. So, will this make Cuba cease to be communist, or is this a real change, or is it just temporary? How should we think about these economic reforms? Is this a real change? Minister: How would you describe a communist economy? Journalist: Well, an economy that the State has basically total control over. Minister: Well, in communism there is supposed to be no state. Journalist: Is there no state in communism? Minister: That’s what Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote, and that’s what Marxists think. Journalist: You know much better than I do. Minister: No, because you’re asking from a place of prejudice or a slogan—which I hope hasn’t influenced the New York Times—that labels Cuba as communist: “Communist Cuba,” “a communist regime,” “a communist economy.” This is completely wrong from both a theoretical and practical standpoint. You could then ask about a socialist Cuba, a socialist economy, and so on. Journalist: Isn’t Cuba communist? Minister: Cuba is not communist, nor could it be. Just as there has never been, nor is there today, any communist state on the planet. Secondly, yes, there are socialist states. There are some with which the current US government has an excellent relationship. There are Asian socialist states with which the United States has a very intense economic, commercial, and investment relationship. They have a true economic interdependence, and I think that’s perfectly fine. And that highlights once again the double standard in American politics, which has excellent relations with other socialist countries or socialist states and also has excellent relations with other countries that are not socialist, but which have a political system that has nothing to do with so-called American democracy. Not only because there is no pluralism of political parties, but because there are none at all, for example. So, what I mean is that the profound economic changes being introduced in Cuba, the profound changes in the Cuban economic model, as I mentioned before, will continue to be focused on the well-being of the population, particularly families and people with lower incomes. It will continue to be centered on social policies with universal coverage, universal protection for our population, which is what has brought us to this point, but these policies entail significant modifications, especially in the distribution of financial and material resources in the country. This includes the continued development of the private sector in Cuba, which is gradually increasing its weight in the Cuban economy. This includes new facilities, incentives, and new conditions—more advantageous conditions, I would say—for foreign counterparties, for direct capital investment in Cuba, for the management of Cuban assets, and for leveraging the comparative advantages that Cuba offers to foreign counterparties. But the Cuban economy will remain socialist. The Cuban model will remain socialist. Like some very successful Asian socialist economies with close economic ties to the United States, the well-being and dignity of human beings will always remain fundamental. But you are right that privatizing some state-owned enterprises is not out of the question, as is already happening to some extent. Part of that process is the conversion to equity capital or contributions from corporations and state-owned enterprises. In some sectors, as everywhere in the world, government entities will seek to acquire controlling shares. State-owned enterprises will also seek to acquire controlling shares. This is the case, for example, with US railroads, and it also occurs in Switzerland and other sectors in Europe, but it does indeed include additional options for the private sector. But it would be an exaggeration to call this set of changes, this transformation, a privatization process because it is not essentially that. It includes privatizations, but privatization is not what distinguishes the transformation of the economic model, which will continue to plan the distribution of resources through the market with non-administrative financial levers and will give the market an even greater role in formulating economic policies and in the economic model itself. Journalist: Very good, very helpful. I understand better now. Is there anything else that…? Minister: Thank you very much. Journalist: Thank you very much. ********* Translation by Walter Lippmann.
